snp3.4:0.2: Another version of this encounter is recorded in SN 7:9.
snp3.4:2.6: The account in SN 7:9 goes immediately from this question to the Buddha’s response marked at 14.1.
snp3.4:4.3: According to SnA, the “clan” of the run-of-the-mill is the five aggregates; it may also refer to the customs of lineages that don’t follow the noble lineage set out in AN 4:28.
snp3.4:7.4: An apparent reference to Ṛgveda 3.62.10, a verse invoking Sāvitrī (the Sun) recited at the ceremony initiating a young brahman into Vedic study, reserved exclusively for brahmans and much meditated on in the major Upaniṣads. SnA suggests the Buddha’s question surprises Sundarika into suspecting he knows more of brahmanical lore than Sundarika does, prompting his change of tone in the next question; SnA also proposes that the Buddhist equivalent of this three-line, twenty-four-syllable verse is the going-for-refuge formula to the Triple Gem.
snp3.4:9.2: I.e., the original rationale for sacrifice was that its recipient be a pure person. The Buddha gives a related answer to a similar question at Sn 5:3.
snp3.4:14.1: In SN 7:9, the Buddha’s initial response to Sundarika begins here.
snp3.4:14.2: SnA explains that it doesn’t matter what kind of wood is used to make a fire—it burns equally hot and bright regardless. See MN 93.
snp3.4:15.3: In SN 7:9, the exchange between the Buddha and Sundarika ends at this point. There, Sundarika then offers the sacrificial cake; the Buddha refuses it (with the passage that here begins at 32.1) and, as in Sn 1:4, has him throw the offering into water, where it sizzles. Shocked, Sundarika returns, and the Buddha teaches him five further verses on inner versus outer fire, true purity through virtue, and crossing over via truth and the holy life, after which Sundarika likewise asks for Acceptance and the two accounts converge again.
snp3.4:19.4: A play on words: arahati, “deserves,” is related to arahant.
snp3.4:24.3: On the implications of being “everywhere released,” see The Paradox of Becoming, chapter 7.
snp3.4:25.3: According to SnA, the field and site of stress refers to defilements; it could also point to the objects of clinging that form a basis for stress, such as the aggregates, sense media, and properties.
snp3.4:26.1: According to SnA, “seclusion” here means unbinding. See SN 21:10 and SN 35:63.
snp3.4:26.3: “Supports” or “mental objects” translates ārammaṇā. See Ud 8:1, SN 12:64, and SN 22:53.
snp3.4:27.2: On unbinding as the end of phenomena, see AN 10:58 and Sn 5:6.
snp3.4:29.1: For examples of seeing self by means of self (or self by means of not-self, or not-self by means of self), see MN 2.
snp3.4:29.2: A play on words: attā can mean both “self” and “mind,” and both senses are active here.
snp3.4:30.5: “Spirit” translates yakkha, which SnA glosses here simply as “person.” See Sn 4:11, note 4.
snp3.4:36.1: “Boundaries” translates sīmantā. According to SnA this is an epithet for defilement: the territory (sīmā) stands for good manners, and its boundary or end (sīmanta) for the defilements lying outside the realm of good manners. For a different sense of “territory,” see Sn 4:4, note 12.
snp3.4:38.3: The phrase sabba-lokasmiṁ, “in all the world”/“for all the world,” apparently functions as a lamp-word here, doing double duty across both clauses.
